This notebook evaluates a single set of metaprograms for a group of samples.
Metaprograms should be: 

* Non-redundant
* Composed of a mix of samples
* Biologically interpretable 

Additionally, we expect expression of these MPs to be variable within the cells of each sample, and therefore useful in identifying cell states in the original samples. 

The metrics shown here will help evaluate if the identified MPs show these characteristics.

```{r define_functions}
#| warning: FALSE

# helper function for getting jaccard between two vectors
calc_jaccard <- function(vec1, vec2) {
  length(intersect(vec1, vec2)) / length(union(vec1, vec2))
}

# function for getting the jaccard index between two gene sets
geneset_jaccard <- function(geneset1, geneset2, geneset_map = all_term_df) {
  
  genes1 <- geneset_map |> 
    dplyr::filter(gs_name == geneset1) |> 
    dplyr::pull(ensembl_gene)
  
  genes2 <- geneset_map |> 
    dplyr::filter(gs_name == geneset2) |> 
    dplyr::pull(ensembl_gene)
  
  jaccard <- calc_jaccard(genes1, genes2)
  
  return(jaccard)
}

# make a heatmap looking at the Jaccard index betwen gene sets for each MP
ora_jaccard_heatmap <- function(results_df, title){
  # only one list here since we will compare each MP to all other MPs
  id1_list <- split(results_df$ID, results_df$metaprogram)
  # create the grid of comparisons
  cross_df <- tidyr::expand_grid(id1 = names(id1_list), id2 = names(id1_list))
  
  # calculate a single Jaccard index for each combination using split lists & ids
  jaccard_scores <- cross_df |>
    purrr::pmap_dbl(\(id1, id2){
      calc_jaccard(id1_list[[id1]], id1_list[[id2]])
    })
  
  # add scores to the comparison grid and convert to matrix
  jaccard_matrix <- cross_df |>
    dplyr::mutate(jaccard = jaccard_scores) |>
    # convert to matrix
    tidyr::pivot_wider(
      names_from = "id2",
      values_from = "jaccard"
    ) |>
    tibble::column_to_rownames(var = "id1") |>
    as.matrix()
  
  ComplexHeatmap::Heatmap(jaccard_matrix,
                          name = "Jaccard index",
                          column_title = title,
                          col = circlize::colorRamp2(c(0, max(jaccard_matrix)), colors = c("white", "darkslateblue")))  
}

# make a dotplot for ORA results from a single metaprogram 
# modified from what we get with enrichplot::dotplot to take as input a dataframe 
dotplot <- function(df, title = NULL) {
  
  df <- df |>
    # only show the top 10 results
    dplyr::slice_min(order_by = p.adjust, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      # convert GeneRatio to a numeric 
      top_number = stringr::word(GeneRatio, 1, sep = "/") |> as.numeric(),
      bottom_number = stringr::word(GeneRatio, -1, sep = "/") |> as.numeric(),
      GeneRatio = top_number/ bottom_number,
      # reformat the description shown for y labels 
      # remove _, wrap and reorder by GeneRatio
      Description = stringr::str_replace_all(Description, "_", " ") |> 
        stringr::str_wrap(width = 30) |> 
        forcats::fct_reorder(GeneRatio)
        
      )

  ggplot2::ggplot(df, aes(
    x     = GeneRatio,
    y     = Description,
    color = p.adjust,
    size  = Count
  )) +
    geom_point() +
    scale_color_continuous(
      low = "#e06663", high = "#327eba",
      name = "p.adjust",
      guide = guide_colorbar(reverse = TRUE)
    ) +
    scale_size(range = c(2, 10)) +
    labs(title = title, x = "GeneRatio", y = NULL) 
}

# helper function to calculate anova on a dataframe
# copied from https://github.com/AlexsLemonade/ews-nf/blob/main/exploratory-notebooks/08-cell-scoring-metrics.Rmd
calculate_anova <- function(df, random_effect = NULL){
  if (!is.null(random_effect)) {
    # create formula with random effect
    formula <- as.formula(glue::glue("log_mean_mp_score ~ disease_timing + (1 | {random_effect})"))
    mod <- lmerTest::lmer(formula, data = df)
    # Overall p-value for disease_timing (type III ANOVA)
    anova_res <- anova(mod) |>
      as.data.frame() |>
      tibble::rownames_to_column("term")
  } else {
    # no random effect so use a regular ANOVA
    mod <- lm(log_mean_mp_score ~ disease_timing, data = df)
    anova_res <- anova(mod) |>
      as.data.frame() |>
      tibble::rownames_to_column("term") |>
      dplyr::filter(term != "Residuals")
  }
  
  return(anova_res)
}

# ANOVA test with/without random effect on log(mean mp score)
# copied from https://github.com/AlexsLemonade/ews-nf/blob/main/exploratory-notebooks/08-cell-scoring-metrics.Rmd
grouped_anova <- function(data, sig_value, random_effect = NULL) {
  
  # for each metaprogram for each value of k, use a linear mixed effect model 
  # then use ANOVA to calculate pvalues 
  anova_results <- data |>
    dplyr::group_by(metaprogram) |>
    # using a lambda function requires two arguments
    # can use ... to absorb the second one
    dplyr::group_modify(\(df, ...) {
      calculate_anova(df, random_effect)
    }) |>
    # classify as significant or not
    dplyr::rename(f_value = `F value`, p_value = `Pr(>F)`) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      p_adj = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH"),
      p_adj_signif = dplyr::if_else(p_adj <= sig_value, "*", "ns")
    ) 
  
  full_results <- anova_results |>
    # join with data/scores for plotting 
    dplyr::left_join(
      data |>
        # we'll plot with zscore so want to use that to determine the y position of the label
        dplyr::summarize(
          max_mean_score = max(zscore_mean_mp_score, na.rm = TRUE),
          .by = c("metaprogram")
        )
    )
  
  return(full_results)
}
```

## Redundancy of metaprograms

Here we look at the correlation of all MPs to all other MPs. 
Ideally, MPs are unique and non-redundant and therefore have low correlation to all other MPs. 
The first plot shows all the spectra that comprise the MPs correlation to all other spectra and the second looks at correlation of each MP to all other MPs.

```{r}
# define colors for the cluster annotations
mp_colors <- palette.colors(n = length(mp_obj$cluster_list), palette = "alphabet") |> 
  purrr::set_names(names(mp_obj$cluster_list))

# metaprogram/cluster annotation
annotation <- ComplexHeatmap::HeatmapAnnotation(
  metaprogram = sprintf("MP%02d", mp_obj$clusters),
  col = list(
    metaprogram = mp_colors
))


# get dendrogram 
dist_mtx <- as.dist(1-cor_mtx)
tree <- hclust(dist_mtx, method = "ward.D2")
dend <- as.dendrogram(tree)

ComplexHeatmap::Heatmap(
  cor_mtx, 
  show_row_names = FALSE, 
  show_column_names = FALSE, 
  cluster_rows = dend,
  cluster_columns = dend,
  top_annotation = annotation,
  name = "correlation"
)
```


```{r}
# combine all mps into a matrix for a heatmap
# get correlation to each other
mp_mtx <- do.call(cbind, mp_obj$metaprogram_list)
mp_cor_matrix <- cor(mp_mtx, method = "pearson", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

annotation <- ComplexHeatmap::HeatmapAnnotation(
  metaprogram = colnames(mp_mtx),
  col = list(
    metaprogram = mp_colors
))

ComplexHeatmap::Heatmap(
  mp_cor_matrix,
  name = "Correlation",
  top_annotation = annotation
)
```


Next we will look at the correlation of each spectra to all other spectra within the same MP and across MPs. 
Ideally, the spectra within a single MP should have high correlation to each other and low correlation to spectra from other MPs.
In the top left corner of each panel the difference in the median between the two groups (within and between MPs) is displayed. 


```{r}
# convert the mp cluster list into a dataframe with one row per spectra
# use this to get the assigned mp for each cluster when calculating metrics
mp_lookup <- tibble::enframe(mp_obj$cluster_list, name = "metaprogram", value = "spectra") |> 
  tidyr::unnest_longer(spectra)

# for each correlation, add in the MPs being compared and classify MP
mp_cor_df <- all_cor_df |> 
  dplyr::filter(spectra1 != spectra2) |> 
  dplyr::left_join(mp_lookup, by = c("spectra1" = "spectra")) |> 
  dplyr::rename(mp1 = metaprogram) |> 
  dplyr::left_join(mp_lookup, by = c("spectra2" = "spectra")) |> 
  dplyr::rename(mp2 = metaprogram) |>
  dplyr::mutate(within_mp = mp1 == mp2) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(mp_comparison_group = dplyr::if_else(within_mp, "Within MP", "Between MPs"),
                spectra_comparison_group = dplyr::case_when(
                  spectra1 == spectra2 ~ "self",
                  spectra1 < spectra2 ~ "different",
                  spectra1 > spectra2 ~ "different_dup"
                )) |> 
  # only report comparisons between different spectra
  # and remove duplicates
  dplyr::filter(spectra_comparison_group == "different") |> 
  dplyr::select(spectra1, spectra2, mp1, mp2, correlation, mp_comparison_group) |> 
  dplyr::distinct()
```


```{r}
# calculate the difference in medians between the two groups to display on the plot
mp_labels <- mp_cor_df |> 
  dplyr::group_by(mp1, mp_comparison_group) |> 
  dplyr::summarise(
    group_median = median(correlation)
  ) |> 
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    id_cols = mp1,
    names_from = mp_comparison_group,
    values_from = group_median
  ) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    median_diff = round(`Within MP` - `Between MPs`, 2),
    x = -Inf, y = Inf
  ) 
```

```{r}
#| fig.width: 8

ggplot(mp_cor_df, aes(x = correlation, color = mp_comparison_group, fill = mp_comparison_group)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.25) +
  facet_wrap(vars(mp1), scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Within MP" = "#00274C", 
                                "Between MPs" = "#FFCB05")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Within MP" = "#00274C", 
                               "Between MPs" = "#FFCB05")) +
  labs(x = "Correlation",
       y = "Density",
       fill = "MP comparison group",
       color = "MP comparison group") +
  geom_text(
    data = mp_labels,
    aes(x = x, y = y, label = median_diff),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    hjust = -0.1, vjust = 1.2,
    size = 4
  )
```


## Sample diversity 

MPs should represent a mix of samples.
This metric can be useful in filtering out any MPs that are sample-specific. 

We will use Shannon's entropy to measure the diversity of each MP where a normalized value of 1 indicates high diversity. 
Shannon's entropy is then used to calculate the normalized effective sample size or Hill number of order 1. 
This represents the effective number of common or abundant samples.
The values are normalized by the total number of samples in the metaprogram such that values close to 1 indicate all samples are equally abundant.

```{r}
# pull out metrics since we'll use this here and for score CVs
mp_metrics_df <- mp_metrics$mp_metrics_df

# grab shannons entropy and effective sample size from metrics 
mp_metrics_df |>
  dplyr::select(
    metaprogram, 
    num_samples, 
    proportion_of_samples,
    num_patients,
    proportion_of_patients,
    shannon_entropy_norm,
    eff_number_norm
  ) |>
  DT::datatable(colnames = c("Metaprogram", "Num Samples", "% Samples", "Num Patients", "% Patients", "Normalized Shannon's Entropy", "Normalized Effective Sample Size")
  ) |> 
  DT::formatPercentage(c("proportion_of_samples", "proportion_of_patients")) |> 
  DT::formatRound(c("shannon_entropy_norm", "eff_number_norm"))
```

The chart below shows the proportion of spectra from each metaprogram that are derived from individual samples. 
Each box represents a unique sample and the length of the box represent the number of spectra from that sample that contribute to the overall metaprogram.

```{r}
# add sample Id column to metaprogram/spectra map
mp_lookup <- mp_lookup |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    sample_id = stringr::str_extract(spectra, "SCPCS[0-9]{6}")
  )

total_samples <- mp_metrics$total_samples

mp_prop_df <- mp_lookup |> 
  dplyr::group_by(metaprogram, sample_id) |>
  # generate one row per mp/sample combination with the total count
  dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n(), 
                   .groups = "drop_last") |> 
  # get the frequency of each sample compared to all other samples
  dplyr::mutate(p = n / sum(n),
                num_samples = dplyr::n_distinct(sample_id)
  ) |> 
  # ungroup before setting levels otherwise the plot doesn't work
  dplyr::ungroup() |> 
  dplyr::mutate(metaprogram = forcats::fct_reorder(metaprogram, num_samples))

ggplot(mp_prop_df, aes(x = p, y = metaprogram, fill = sample_id)) +
  geom_col(color = "gray70") +
  labs(
    y = "Metaprogram",
    x = "Proportion of spectra",
    fill = "Sample"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "none"
  )
```

## Biological interpretability 

Ultimately, we want to be able to easily interpret the MPs. 
We won't actually annotate them here, but we will look to see how biologically distinct the MPs might be. 

To do that, we'll take the first 200 genes for all MPs and do ORA using the custom genesets we use for classifying EWS::FLI1 high and low cells, the Hallmarks collection from `MSigDb`, and the Reactome gene set from `MSigDb`. 

```{r}
# pull out the top genes and ora results from metrics df
ora_results_df <- mp_metrics$ora_results_df
mp_top_list <- mp_metrics$top_genes
```

```{r}
#| results: 'asis'

# print out a message about which MPs have 0 genesets 
all_mps <- names(mp_top_list)
missing_mps <- all_mps[!all_mps %in% unique(ora_results_df$metaprogram)] |> 
  paste0(collapse = ", ")

if(missing_mps != "") {
  glue::glue("
      <div class=\"alert alert-info\">

      No gene sets were identified as significant in the following metaprograms: 
      {missing_mps}
      </div>
    ")
  }
```


To evaluate if the MPs are easily interpretable, we will make a heatmap that shows the significance of each gene set across all MPs. 
Ideal MPs will show gene sets that are uniquely enriched in that MP instead of enriched across multiple MPs. 
The rows represent the all significant gene sets, the columns indicate the MP, and the heatmap color indicates the -log10(pvalue) for that gene set in that MP.
Only the top 5 gene sets for each metaprogram are shown to save space.

Only MPs with identified gene sets will be included. 

```{r}
#| fig.height: 10
#| fig.width: 22


# convert ora results into a heatmap of pvalues
heatmap_mtx <- ora_results_df |> 
  dplyr::mutate(logp = -log10(p.adjust)) |> 
  # only keep the top 10 gene sets
  dplyr::slice_max(logp, n = 5, by = metaprogram) |>
  dplyr::select(metaprogram, ID, logp) |> 
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = metaprogram,
    values_from = logp,
    values_fill = 0  # set missing gene sets to 0                         
  ) |> 
  # remove _ and wrap gene set names
  dplyr::mutate(
    ID = stringr::str_replace_all(ID, "_", " ") |> 
      stringr::str_wrap(width = 33)
  ) |> 
  tibble::column_to_rownames("ID") |> 
  as.matrix() |> 
  t()

ComplexHeatmap::Heatmap(
  heatmap_mtx,
  name = "-log10(pvalue)\n",
  row_names_side = "left",
  row_dend_side = "right",
  cluster_rows = FALSE,
  col = circlize::colorRamp2(c(0, max(heatmap_mtx)), colors = c("white", "darkslateblue")),
  row_names_gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = 20),
  column_names_gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = 16),
  heatmap_legend_param = list(
    title_gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = 20),
    labels_gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = 20)
  )
) |> 
  # don't cut off super long gene set names
  ComplexHeatmap::draw(padding = unit(c(6, 2, 2, 2), "cm"))
```

Alternatively, we can use the Jaccard similarity to index to measure how similar the list of gene sets for each MP is to all other MPs. 


```{r}
ora_jaccard_heatmap(ora_results_df,
                    title = "All gene sets")
```


The custom EF-activated and EF-repressed gene sets are likely to be found in more than 1 module as all of these cells should exhibit some level of EWS::FLI1 activity. 
To look at the uniqueness of non-EWS::FLI1 gene sets we will re-calculate the Jaccard index for all other gene sets. 

```{r}
# get the EF activated and EF repressed gene sets
ef_activated_genesets <- ef_category_df |> 
  dplyr::filter(geneset_category == "EF-activated") |> 
  dplyr::pull(full_geneset_name)

ef_repressed_genesets <- ef_category_df |> 
  dplyr::filter(geneset_category == "EF-repressed") |> 
  dplyr::pull(full_geneset_name)

# remove ef gene sets for jaccard calculations
# we expect some overlap of these already so let's see how unique the remaining genesets are
filtered_ora_results_df <- ora_results_df |> 
  dplyr::filter(!ID %in% c(ef_repressed_genesets, ef_activated_genesets))

ora_jaccard_heatmap(filtered_ora_results_df,
                    title = "EF gene sets removed")
```

### Specificity and similarity of gene sets

Here we will look at the identified gene sets for each metaprogram. 
If multiple gene sets are returned, it's likely that they are biologically similar. 
Having multiple gene sets that are biologically distinct is going to impede interpretation.
This plot shows all gene sets, including EWS::FLI1 gene sets.

```{r}
#| fig.height: 25
#| fig.width: 15

# dot plots for all mps with at least 1 significant gene set
split(ora_results_df, ora_results_df$metaprogram) |> 
  purrr::imap(\(result, mp){
    if(nrow(result) > 0) {
      dotplot(result, title = mp)
    }
  }) |> 
  purrr::compact() |>
  patchwork::wrap_plots(ncol = 2)
```


### Ewing specific gene sets

We know that these tumor cells should show have a group of cells with a EWS::FLI1 repressed cell signature, or "low", as we have been calling them. 
To see if any of these MPs show that signature, we'll get a score for whether or not that MP shows a high or low signature.
This is calculated by getting the sum of all significant gene sets in either the EF-activated or EF-repressed gene sets and then dividing by the total number of gene sets in that group. 


```{r}
ora_results_df |> 
  dplyr::mutate(ef_high = ID %in% ef_activated_genesets,
                ef_low = ID %in% ef_repressed_genesets) |> 
  dplyr::summarize(
    ef_high_score = round(sum(ef_high)/length(ef_activated_genesets), 2),
    ef_low_score = round(sum(ef_low)/length(ef_repressed_genesets),2),
    .by = "metaprogram"
  ) |> 
  DT::datatable()
```

## Using metaprograms to identify cell states 

Ultimately we want to be able to use these MPs to identify cell states in our original data. 
In order to do that, we need to assign a score to each cell for each MP and then use that to pull out cells with high scores for that MP. 
Good MPs should show variation in scores across samples. 

Score were assigned for each cell by getting the dot product between the weights for the top 200 genes in the MP and the normalized gene expression values.
Before calculating the score, gene expression was quantile normalized within each sample.

First we look at the score distribution for all samples for each metaprogram. 
Good MPs will show variability within the dataset, in particular we are looking for a bimodal distribution.

```{r}
#| message: FALSE
#| warning: FALSE

ggplot(score_df, 
       aes(x = mp_score, y = forcats::fct_rev(metaprogram))) +
  ggridges::geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.8, color = "white", rel_min_height = 0.01) +
  #facet_wrap(vars(sample_id), scales = "free_x", ncol = 4) +
  theme(
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey90"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.position = "none"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Score across all samples",
    y = "Metaprogram"
  ) +
  xlim(c(0,0.5))
```

Good metaprograms should show variation in the scores assigned to cells in the original dataset.
To measure variation, we will use the coefficient of variation (CV), which reports a score's variance relative to the mean score across all cells. 

```{r}
# calculate the variance for each MP in each sample
mp_var_df <- score_df |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    variance = stats::var(mp_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    cv = sqrt(variance) / mean(mp_score),
    .by = c("sample_id", "metaprogram")
  )

ggplot(
  mp_var_df,
  aes(
    x = metaprogram,
    y = cv
  )
) +
  ggforce::geom_sina(size = 1, alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(
    x = "Metaprogram",
    y = "CV across all cells in a sample"
  )

```

Now, we'll look at the distribution for each sample individually. 
Good MPs should show variability in multiple samples. 

```{r}
#| fig.height: 35
#| fig.width: 12
#| message: FALSE
#| warning: FALSE 


ggplot(score_df, 
       aes(x = mp_score, y = metaprogram, fill = metaprogram)) +
  ggridges::geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.8, color = "white", bw = 0.5, rel_min_height = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(vars(sample_id), scales = "free_x", ncol = 4) +
  theme(
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey90"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 6),
    legend.position = "none"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Score",
    y = "Metaprogram",
    title = "MP scores by sample"
  )
```

### Comparison of scores across sample types 
<!--Code and text are adapted from the Comparison of scores across sample types section in the combined metrics report-->

Here we look at the distribution of cell scores across varying sample types (primary, metastatic, and recurrent tumors). 
First, we calculate the mean score for each metaprogram for each sample. 
As the scores are skewed towards zero, we log-transform the scores before calculating any statistics. 
We then compare scores to determine if any metaprograms show significantly different distributions across sample types. 
For the statistical test, we use a linear mixed model with patient as the random effect to account for within-patient correlation that is likely observed among different sample types from the same patient. 

For visualization purposes, we calculate a z-score for all `log(mean(scores))` within each metaprogram and display that in the box plot below.
The significance of the comparison among the three sample types is shown above the distributions for that metaprogram with `*` indicating that the distributions are significantly different from each other and `ns` indicating the distributions are not significantly different from each other. 

```{r}
# copied from https://github.com/AlexsLemonade/ews-nf/blob/main/templates/combined-metaprogram-metrics.Rmd
# adapted to not consider n_metaprograms since here we just have one value of k 

mean_scores_df <- score_df |> 
  dplyr::summarize(
    mean_mp_score = mean(mp_score),
    .by = c("unique_id", "metaprogram")
  ) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    scpca_sample_id = stringr::word(unique_id, -1, sep = "-"),
    # first log transform
    log_mean_mp_score = log(mean_mp_score)
  ) |>
  # z-score the log scores within each k and metaprogram
  # use these for plotting
  dplyr::mutate(
    zscore_mean_mp_score = scale(log_mean_mp_score), 
    .by = c("metaprogram")
  ) |> 
  # add in the sample metadata including disease timing and patient information 
  dplyr::left_join(
    dplyr::select(
      sample_df, 
      c("scpca_sample_id", "participant_id", "disease_timing")
    ), 
    by = c("scpca_sample_id")
  )
```

```{r}
#| message: FALSE 
# calculate anova with random effect
random_effect_lmm_results <- grouped_anova(mean_scores_df, sig_value = 0.05, random_effect = "participant_id")
```

```{r}
# plot the scores fore ach sample type and indicate the significance
ggplot(mean_scores_df, aes(x = metaprogram, y = zscore_mean_mp_score, fill = disease_timing)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.1) +
  geom_text(
    data = random_effect_lmm_results,
    color = "red",
    aes(x = metaprogram, y = max_mean_score + 0.3, label = p_adj_signif),
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = disease_timing_palette) +
  labs(
    title = "ANOVA with patient as random effect",
    fill = "Sample type",
    x = "Metaprogram",
    y = "Z-score computed from \nmean metaprogram score per sample"
  )
```
